prize_parts.citation: for empirical and conceptual analysis of how trade exposure and technological change reshape local labour markets, labour demand and wage inequality

statement.case_for: B038 meets the criterion of a specific scientific contribution that combines new evidence with an explanatory framework. The China-shock papers measure how import exposure changed employment, wages and adjustment in local labour markets. The task-based account explains why technology changes the demand for different kinds of work and why wage structures polarise. The work reshaped research in labour, trade and public economics, and it moved policy debate on globalisation and automation. Its influence runs through the research itself and the large literature it inspired. It has had more than a decade of replication, critique and extension, so durability can be judged. The local-labour-market design has been absorbed into standard practice, even though the magnitude and persistence of the effects are still debated. Among the candidates I find the empirical design and the conceptual payoff most visibly joined here. I put it ahead of B002 mainly on maturity and on how independently the findings can be checked.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and coherence. The China-shock results belong cleanly to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The task framework has a wider lineage that this ballot entry only partly captures, and part of that lineage sits with scholars who are not credited or who were recognised in 2024. A citation that bundles trade shocks and tasks may look like two contributions under one name, and a three-person cap forces an arguable choice. Shift-share identification has been criticised, and the persistence and external validity of the local effects remain contested. If the Committee judges the trade-shock evidence too narrow or too contested, B002 or B007 would have the stronger claim.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B038 second but proposes Katz in place of Dorn, because Katz has long-running contributions on skill demand and wage structure. He also notes that credit for the task framework extends beyond the credited names and that the shift-share design has been criticised.
responses.response: I take the lineage point seriously, and I agree that Katz's work on the race between education and technology is foundational for wage structure. But the citation I propose rests on the local labour-market evidence on trade and technology exposure. That evidence is the joint product of Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and Dorn is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers. Replacing him with Katz would credit a different strand and would leave the core papers incompletely attributed. Katz also appears on B002, so it would be inconsistent to place him here and treat him as secondary there. I accept that a Katz-based version is defensible if the Committee wants a wider wage-inequality prize. On shift-share, I read the debate as having been absorbed rather than as having overturned the findings, but I agree that magnitudes remain uncertain.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B038 seventh. He doubts that the shift-share identification strategy withstands current scrutiny, sees overlap with recent technology prizes, and notes that the task framework owes a debt to authors who are not listed.
responses.response: The identification criticism is legitimate, and it is the main reason I do not claim the magnitudes are settled. But the criticism concerns inference and exposure design. The qualitative finding of large and persistent local adjustment costs has survived reanalysis, and the debate has produced better practice. Judged against common criteria, a contribution that has stimulated its own methodological scrutiny and survived it is a point in its favour. I agree on the overlap risk, which I list as an uncertainty. Still, the 2024 prize addressed institutions and growth, not local labour-market adjustment to trade, so I do not see the same ground covered. I would not call B038 less mature than your top-ranked B030, where the core methods are older but their reach is narrower.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B002 first, with Chetty and Hendren as the core. She emphasises that large samples, transparent measurement and credible quasi-experimental designs make the findings comparatively robust, and she ranks B038 second.
responses.response: I agree that B002 is a very strong candidate. It is the one I rank closest to my first choice, and I list it as my main alternative. We part on timing and verifiability. Most of the mobility results date from 2014 onwards, and they rest heavily on restricted administrative data that few outside the group can replicate. The long-run causal reading of place effects is still being tested. B038 has had a longer period of independent replication and critique. I would also point out that your two-name proposal for B002 sidesteps the Friedman and Katz question that the three-name versions face, which suggests the attribution there is less settled than the robust-measurement argument implies. If the Committee prefers to reward the data-infrastructure advance now, I could support B002 with Chetty, Hendren and Friedman.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants a prize built on the trade-shock evidence, on the task and wage-structure framework, or on both, and how that choice should settle the third name between Dorn and Katz.
How much of the task-based lineage belongs to scholars outside the credited names, and whether the 2024 recognition of technology and institutions narrows the room for this topic.
How persistent and how externally valid the China-shock effects are, and whether the criticism of shift-share designs will change the reading of the core results.
Whether B002 is mature enough to rank above B038, given its reliance on restricted data and its concentration of credit in one research group.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the shortlisted candidates appears among my listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler). I work in labour economics with quasi-experimental methods, which may incline me to favour B038 and B002. I flag that as field familiarity, not as evidence of merit.
